claim: Cortical asymmetry is a ubiquitous feature of brain organization that is subtly altered in some neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Cortical asymmetry is a ubiquitous feature of brain organization that is subtly altered in some neurodevelopmental disorders, yet we lack knowledge of how its development proceeds across life in health.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature on cortical asymmetry and neurodevelopmental disorders.

claim: Areal asymmetry is predominantly stable across life.
source: Whereas areal asymmetry is predominantly stable across life, thickness asymmetry grows in childhood and peaks in early adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by the longitudinal lifespan trajectory analyses presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Thickness asymmetry grows in childhood and peaks in early adulthood.
source: Whereas areal asymmetry is predominantly stable across life, thickness asymmetry grows in childhood and peaks in early adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by the longitudinal lifespan trajectory analyses presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Areal asymmetry is low-moderately heritable with maximum h2SNP approximately 19%.
source: Areal asymmetry is low-moderately heritable (max h2SNP ~19%) and correlates phenotypically and genetically in specific regions, indicating coordinated development of asymmetries partly through genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by SNP-based heritability analyses in UK Biobank data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Thickness asymmetry is globally interrelated across the cortex in a pattern suggesting highly left-lateralized individuals tend towards left-lateralization also in population-level right-asymmetric regions (and vice versa).
source: In contrast, thickness asymmetry is globally interrelated across the cortex in a pattern suggesting highly left-lateralized individuals tend towards left-lateralization also in population-level right-asymmetric regions (and vice versa), and exhibits low or absent heritability.
evidence: This claim is supported by interregional correlation analyses presented in Figure 5.

claim: Thickness asymmetry exhibits low or absent heritability.
source: In contrast, thickness asymmetry is globally interrelated across the cortex in a pattern suggesting highly left-lateralized individuals tend towards left-lateralization also in population-level right-asymmetric regions (and vice versa), and exhibits low or absent heritability.
evidence: This claim is supported by heritability analyses presented in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1I.

claim: Less areal asymmetry in the most consistently lateralized region in humans associates with subtly lower cognitive ability.
source: We find less areal asymmetry in the most consistently lateralized region in humans associates with subtly lower cognitive ability, and confirm small handedness and sex effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by association analyses in UK Biobank data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Areal asymmetry is developmentally stable and arises early in life through genetic but mainly subject-specific stochastic effects.
source: Results suggest areal asymmetry is developmentally stable and arises early in life through genetic but mainly subject-specific stochastic effects, whereas childhood developmental growth shapes thickness asymmetry and may lead to directional variability of global thickness lateralization in the population.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on the combined findings of lifespan stability, low-moderate heritability, and early establishment of areal asymmetry.

claim: Childhood developmental growth shapes thickness asymmetry and may lead to directional variability of global thickness lateralization in the population.
source: Results suggest areal asymmetry is developmentally stable and arises early in life through genetic but mainly subject-specific stochastic effects, whereas childhood developmental growth shapes thickness asymmetry and may lead to directional variability of global thickness lateralization in the population.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on the combined findings of developmental growth trajectories, low heritability, and global interrelations of thickness asymmetry.

claim: The brain's hemispheres exhibit high contralateral symmetry.
source: The brain's hemispheres exhibit high contralateral symmetry (van Kesteren and Kievit, 2021; Stark et al., 2008), homotopic regions are under similar genetic influence (Schmitt et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2013; Eyler et al., 2014) and show highly correlated developmental change (Schmitt et al., 2018; Raznahan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Structural asymmetry is a ubiquitous aspect of brain organization.
source: Despite this, structural asymmetry is also a ubiquitous aspect of brain organization (Kong et al., 2018; Chiarello et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortical thickness and surface area are known to exhibit distinct asymmetry patterns.
source: Cortical thickness and surface area are known to exhibit distinct asymmetry patterns (Kong et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2014), albeit reported inconsistently (Kong et al., 2018; Chiarello et al., 2016; Roe et al., 2021; Li et al., 2015; Luders et al., 2006; Lyttelton et al., 2009; Sha et al., 2021a; Zhou et al., 2013; Maingault et al., 2016; Shaw et al., 2009; Lou et al., 2020; Hamilton et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2018; Koelkebeck et al., 2014; Plessen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At least some aspects of cortical asymmetry are confirmed to be subtly reduced in neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism.
source: Although an extensive literature in search of structural asymmetry deviations in various conditions and disorders is in several cases being challenged by newer data (Kong et al., 2022), at least some aspects of cortical asymmetry are confirmed to be subtly reduced in neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism (Postema et al., 2019; Sha et al., 2022), but also through later life influences such as aging, and Alzheimer's disease (Roe et al., 2021; Thompson et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No previous study has charted cortical asymmetry trajectories from childhood to old age using longitudinal data.
source: However, it is currently unknown how cortical asymmetry development proceeds across life in health, because no previous study has charted cortical asymmetry trajectories from childhood to old age using longitudinal data.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' review of the literature and establishes the novelty of their study.

claim: Previous large-scale studies do not delineate the precise brain regions exhibiting robust cortical asymmetry, relying on brain atlases with predefined anatomical boundaries that may not conform well to the underlying asymmetry of cortex.
source: Compounding the lack of longitudinal investigation, previous large-scale studies do not delineate the precise brain regions exhibiting robust cortical asymmetry, relying on brain atlases with predefined anatomical boundaries that may not conform well to the underlying asymmetry of cortex (Kong et al., 2018; Sha et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and establishes a methodological limitation of previous studies.

claim: Indirect evidence in neonates suggests adult-like patterns of areal asymmetry are evident at birth.
source: For areal asymmetry, surprisingly few studies have charted developmental (Li et al., 2014; Remer et al., 2017) or aging-related effects (Kong et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2022), although indirect evidence in neonates suggests adult-like patterns of areal asymmetry are evident at birth (Li et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2023) and may exhibit little change from birth to 2 years (Li et al., 2014) despite rapid and concurrent developmental cortical expansion (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on neonatal brain development.

claim: Longitudinal increases in thickness asymmetry have been shown during the first two years of life.
source: For thickness asymmetry, longitudinal increases in asymmetry have been shown during the first two years of life (Li et al., 2015), with suggestions of rapid asymmetry growth from birth to 1 year (Li et al., 2015), and potentially continued growth until adolescence (Nie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on early brain development.

claim: Previous lifespan studies mapped thickness asymmetry linearly across cross-sectional developmental and adult age-ranges, mostly concluding thickness asymmetry is minimal in infancy and maximal age ~60.
source: However, previous lifespan studies mapped thickness asymmetry linearly across cross-sectional developmental and adult age-ranges (Zhou et al., 2013; Plessen et al., 2014), mostly concluding thickness asymmetry is minimal in infancy and maximal age ~60.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and establishes a limitation of previous studies.

claim: Recent work established thickness asymmetry shows a non-linear decline from 20 to 90 years that is reproducible across longitudinal aging cohorts.
source: In contrast, recent work established thickness asymmetry shows a non-linear decline from 20 to 90 years that is reproducible across longitudinal aging cohorts (Roe et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Contemporary research suggests brain asymmetries are complex, multifactorial and independent (i.e. uncorrelated) traits.
source: Contemporary research suggests brain asymmetries are complex, multifactorial and independent (i.e. uncorrelated) traits (Rentería, 2012; Francks, 2015; Neubauer et al., 2020), contrasting earlier theories emphasizing a single (Annett, 1998; Annett, 1964) or predominating factor controlling various cerebral lateralizations (McManus and Bryden, 1991; Geschwind and Galaburda, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Evidence suggests cortical asymmetries are mostly independent.
source: Where reported, evidence suggests cortical asymmetries are mostly independent (Sha et al., 2021b; Guadalupe et al., 2015; Chiarello et al., 2013) – in line with a multifactorial view (Bain et al., 2019; Rentería, 2012; Francks, 2015; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is currently unknown whether or which cortical asymmetries are reliably correlated within individuals.
source: Currently, it is unknown whether or which cortical asymmetries are reliably correlated within individuals, though this may signify coordinated development of left-right brain asymmetries through genetic or lifespan influences – a genetic or later developmental account depending on trait heritability and whether phenotypic correlations are underpinned by genetic correlations.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' review of the literature and establishes a knowledge gap.

claim: Altered development of cerebral lateralization has been widely hypothesized to relate to average poorer cognitive outcomes.
source: Finally, altered development of cerebral lateralization has been widely hypothesized to relate to average poorer cognitive outcomes (Plessen et al., 2014; Crow et al., 1998; Hirnstein et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Phenotypic asymmetry-cognition associations have been rarely reported, conflicting, not comparable, and to date remain untested in large-scale data.
source: Specifically in the context of cortical asymmetry, however, although one previous study reported larger thickness asymmetry may relate to better verbal and visuospatial cognition (Plessen et al., 2014), phenotypic asymmetry-cognition associations have been rarely reported (Plessen et al., 2014; Moodie et al., 2020; Yeo et al., 2016), conflicting (Moodie et al., 2020; Yeo et al., 2016), not comparable (Plessen et al., 2014; Moodie et al., 2020), and to date remain untested in large-scale data.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and establishes a knowledge gap.

claim: Recent work points to small but significant overlap between genes underlying multivariate brain asymmetries and those influencing educational attainment and specific developmental disorders impacting cognition.
source: Still, recent work points to small but significant overlap between genes underlying multivariate brain asymmetries and those influencing educational attainment and specific developmental disorders impacting cognition (Sha et al., 2021b), indicating either pleiotropy between non-related traits or capturing shared genetic susceptibility to altered brain lateralization and cognitive outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Most large-scale studies examining factors widely assumed important for asymmetry have used brain atlases with limited spatial precision.
source: However, most large-scale studies examining factors widely assumed important for asymmetry have used brain atlases with limited spatial precision (Kong et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2022; Sha et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and establishes a methodological limitation.

claim: Such studies did not detect associations with handedness that were not found until a recent study applied higher resolution (i.e. vertex-wise) mapping in big data.
source: Accordingly, such studies did not detect associations with handedness (Kong et al., 2018; Wiberg et al., 2019) that were not found until a recent study applied higher resolution (i.e. vertex-wise) mapping in big data (Sha et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Areal asymmetries were highly consistent across all 7 datasets.
source: Areal asymmetries were highly consistent across all 7 datasets (Figure 1A): the spatial correlation between surface AI maps ranged from r=0.88 to 0.97 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial correlation analysis presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Overlapping effects for strong leftward areal asymmetry were observed in a large cluster in supramarginal gyrus (SMG) that spanned postcentral gyrus, planum temporale and primary auditory regions.
source: Across all seven datasets (Figure 1D), overlapping effects for strong leftward areal asymmetry were observed in a large cluster in supramarginal gyrus (SMG) that spanned postcentral gyrus, planum temporale and primary auditory regions (and conformed well to their anatomical boundaries; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A for significance), anterior insula and temporal cortex, rostral anterior cingulate, medial superior frontal cortex, and precuneus, the latter spanning parahippocampal and entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlapping effects analysis presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Overlapping effects for strong rightward areal asymmetry were evident in cingulate, inferior parietal cortex, STS, medial occipital cortex, mPFC and rostral middle frontal cortex.
source: Overlapping effects for strong rightward areal asymmetry were evident in cingulate, inferior parietal cortex, STS, medial occipital cortex, medial PFC (mPFC) and rostral middle frontal cortex (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlapping effects analysis presented in Figure 1D.

claim: This global pattern agrees with previous reports.
source: This global pattern agrees with previous reports (Kong et al., 2018; Lyttelton et al., 2009; Sha et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: For thickness, an anterior-posterior pattern of left-right asymmetry was evident in most datasets.
source: For thickness, an anterior-posterior pattern of left-right asymmetry was evident in most datasets (Figure 1B), consistent with more recent reports (Kong et al., 2018; Roe et al., 2021; Sha et al., 2021a; Plessen et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the visual inspection of Figure 1B and citations to prior literature.

claim: Spatial correlations between AI maps from independent datasets were high for thickness asymmetry, but notably more variable than for areal asymmetry.
source: Though spatial correlations between AI maps from independent datasets were high, they were notably more variable (r=0.33 - 0.93; Figure 1C); HCP showed lower correlation with all datasets (r=0.33 - 0.46) whereas all other datasets correlated highly (min r=0.78).
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial correlation analysis presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Consistent leftward thickness asymmetry effects were evident in cingulate, postcentral gyrus, and superior frontal cortex.
source: Consistent leftward thickness asymmetry effects were evident in cingulate, postcentral gyrus, and superior frontal cortex (Figure 1E), whereas consistent effects for rightward thickness asymmetry were evident in a large cluster in and around STS (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), insula, lingual gyrus, parahippocampal and entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlapping effects analysis presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The proportion of individuals lateralized in the population direction in each cluster was highly similar across datasets, on average ranging between 61% and 94% for area, and 57–90% for thickness.
source: The proportion of individuals lateralized in the population direction in each cluster was highly similar across datasets, on average ranging between 61% and 94% for area, and 57–90% for thickness (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis presented in Figure 1F-I.

claim: In all clusters, the homotopic areal trajectories revealed areal asymmetry was strongly established already by age ~4, and the lifespan trajectories of both leftward and rightward asymmetries were largely parallel.
source: In all clusters, the homotopic areal trajectories revealed areal asymmetry was strongly established already by age ~4, and the lifespan trajectories of both leftward (Figure 2A) and rightward (Figure 2B) asymmetries were largely parallel.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lifespan trajectory analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: There was little indication of relative hemispheric differences during cortical developmental expansion from 4 to 30 years for areal asymmetry.
source: There was also little indication of relative hemispheric differences during cortical developmental expansion from 4 to 30 years (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) or aging from 30 to 89 years (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the relative developmental trajectory analysis presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Areal asymmetry was significantly different from zero across the entire lifespan in all clusters.
source: Though lifespan areal asymmetry trajectories did show significant change at some point throughout life in most clusters (Supplementary file 1E), factor-smooth GAMM interaction analyses confirmed that areal asymmetry was significantly different from zero across the entire lifespan in all clusters (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2), and the average trajectories across all leftward and rightward clusters were clearly parallel (although still both exhibited a significant difference; bordered plots in Figure 2A–B; Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GAMM analysis presented in Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Homotopic trajectories of thickness clusters were non-parallel, and mostly characterized by developmental increase in thickness asymmetry from age 4–30, through seemingly unequal rates of continuous thinning between hemispheres.
source: In contrast, though homotopic trajectories of thickness clusters were more variable, they were non-parallel, and mostly characterized by developmental increase in thickness asymmetry from age 4–30, through seemingly unequal rates of continuous thinning between hemispheres (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the lifespan trajectory analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: In 10/20 clusters the data indicated developmental increase in thickness asymmetry corresponded to a significant relative hemispheric difference in the rate of developmental thinning.
source: Importantly, in 10/20 clusters the data indicated developmental increase in thickness asymmetry corresponded to a significant relative hemispheric difference in the rate of developmental thinning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the relative developmental trajectory analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Leftward thickness asymmetry developed through comparatively slower thinning of the LH that was significant in 6 clusters.
source: Mostly, these conformed to a pattern whereby the thicker homotopic hemisphere thinned comparatively slower (Figure 4): leftward thickness asymmetry developed through comparatively slower thinning of the LH that was significant in 6 clusters (superior, lateral and medial PFC #2 #8 #10, precentral #4, inferior temporal #6, calcarine #11; Figure 3A; Figure 4), whereas rightward asymmetry developed through significantly slower RH thinning (STS #1, planum temporale #7, anterior insula #9; Figure 3A; Figure 4), or significantly faster RH thickening (#5 entorhinal).
evidence: This claim is supported by the relative developmental trajectory analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: In these clusters, asymmetry development was generally evident until a peak in early adulthood (median age at peak = 24.3) for both leftward and rightward clusters.
source: In these clusters, asymmetry development was generally evident until a peak in early adulthood (median age at peak = 24.3; see Figure 4) for both leftward and rightward clusters, around a point of inflection to less developmental thinning (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of age at peak asymmetry presented in Figure 4.

claim: 95% of clusters exhibited small but significant asymmetry at age ~4.
source: Despite the developmental growth, factor-smooth GAMMs nevertheless confirmed the developmental foundation for thickness asymmetry was already established by age ~4 (95% of clusters exhibited small but significant asymmetry at age ~4; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), and again asymmetry trajectories showed significant change at some point throughout life (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GAMM analysis presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Across clusters delineated here we observed little evidence aging-related change from 30 to 89 years corresponded to a relative hemispheric difference in the rate of aging-related thinning, except in regions overlapping with our previous report.
source: Across clusters delineated here we observed little evidence aging-related change from 30 to 89 years corresponded to a relative hemispheric difference in the rate of aging-related thinning, except in regions overlapping with our previous report (Roe et al., 2021; e.g. mPFC #10; Figure 3—figure supplement 5B; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the relative aging trajectory analysis presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: For areal asymmetry, a common covariance structure between asymmetries was detectable across datasets: Mantel tests revealed the correlation matrices derived independently in LCBC, UKB and HCP data all correlated almost perfectly (r ≥ 0.97, all p<9.9e-5).
source: For areal asymmetry, a common covariance structure between asymmetries was detectable across datasets: Mantel tests revealed the correlation matrices derived independently in LCBC, UKB and HCP data all correlated almost perfectly (r ≥ 0.97, all p<9.9e-5; Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Mantel test results presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The highest correlations all reflected positive correlations between regions that are on average left-asymmetric and regions that are on average right-asymmetric.
source: The highest correlations (or 'hotspots') all reflected positive correlations between regions that are on average left-asymmetric and regions that are on average right-asymmetric (i.e. higher leftward asymmetry in one region related to higher rightward asymmetry in another; Figure 5A black outline); leftward asymmetry in SMG/perisylvian (#1 L) was related to higher rightward asymmetry in inferior parietal cortex (#2 R; r=0.48 [LCBC]), leftward anterior cingulate asymmetry (ACC; #3 L) was related to higher rightward asymmetry in mPFC (#6 R, r=0.47), and leftward asymmetry in a superior frontal cluster (#7 L) was related to rightward asymmetry in the cingulate (#3 R, r=0.68).
evidence: This claim is supported by the interregional correlation analysis presented in Figure 5A.

claim: None of the relationships could be explained by brain size, as additionally removing the effect of intracranial volume (ICV) from cluster AI's had a negligible effect on their interrelations (max correlation change=0.009).
source: None of the relationships could be explained by brain size, as additionally removing the effect of intracranial volume (ICV) from cluster AI's had a negligible effect on their interrelations (max correlation change=0.009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a control analysis removing ICV effects.

claim: Geodesic distance was lower between cluster-pairs that were more correlated for opposite-direction areal asymmetries.
source: Post-hoc tests confirmed that opposite-direction areal asymmetries were more correlated if closer in cortex (Methods); geodesic distance was lower between cluster-pairs that were more correlated (rho=–0.35, p=0.01 [LCBC]; –0.38, p=0.007 [UKB; Figure 5C]; –0.34, p=0.02 [HCP]), though this was driven by the aforementioned 'hotspots'.
evidence: This claim is supported by the geodesic distance analysis presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Same-direction areal asymmetries were not more correlated if closer in cortex.
source: By contrast, same-direction areal asymmetries were not more correlated if closer in cortex (leftward [all p>0.5]; rightward [all p>0.5]).
evidence: This claim is supported by the geodesic distance analysis.

claim: For thickness asymmetry, the correlation matrix exhibited a clear pattern in UKB that was less visible but still apparent in LCBC and HCP.
source: For thickness asymmetry, the correlation matrix exhibited a clear pattern in UKB that was less visible but still apparent in LCBC and HCP (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the visual inspection of Figure 5B.

claim: Mantel tests confirmed that the covariance structure for thickness asymmetry replicated between all dataset-pairs.
source: Mantel tests confirmed that the covariance structure replicated between all dataset-pairs (LCBC-UKB r=0.49, p=0.007; LCBC-HCP r=0.62, p<2.9e–4; UKB-HCP r=0.46, p=0.009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Mantel test results.

claim: Higher leftward asymmetry in regions that are left-asymmetric actually corresponded to more leftward asymmetry in right-asymmetric regions, and vice versa.
source: However, given that the AI measure is bidirectional, closer inspection of the correlations revealed that higher leftward asymmetry in regions that are left-asymmetric actually corresponded to more leftward asymmetry in right-asymmetric regions, and vice versa (and on average; see Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the detailed inspection of correlations presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Post-hoc principal components analysis (PCA) in UKB revealed PC1 explained 21.9% of the variance in thickness asymmetry and suggested a single component may be evident for thickness asymmetry.
source: Post-hoc principal components analysis (PCA) in UKB revealed PC1 explained 21.9% of the variance in thickness asymmetry and suggested a single component may be evident for thickness asymmetry (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCA analysis presented in Figure 5D.

claim: We found a correlation of r=–0.61 between mean asymmetry across all leftward vs. mean asymmetry across all rightward clusters in UKB.
source: Accordingly, we found a correlation of r=–0.61 between mean asymmetry across all leftward vs. mean asymmetry across all rightward clusters in UKB p<2.2e-16 [means weighted by cluster size]; see Figure 5D; r=–0.56, p<2.2e-16 [unweighted means]; r=0.66, p<2.2e-16 [PC1 across all leftward vs. PC1 across all rightward].
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Heritability of the global measures for each hemisphere was high (area h2SNP ~67%, h2twin ~92%; thickness h2SNP ~36%, h2twin ~81%).
source: Although heritability of the global measures for each hemisphere was high (area h2SNP ~67%, h2twin ~92%; thickness h2SNP ~36%, h2twin ~81%), heritability of global asymmetry measures was substantially lower (area h2SNP=7% [95% CI=3–10%], h2twin=16% [5–27%]; thickness h2SNP=1% [0–5%], h2twin=16% [5–27%]).
evidence: This claim is supported by the heritability analysis.

claim: Heritability of global asymmetry measures was substantially lower (area h2SNP=7% [95% CI=3–10%], h2twin=16% [5–27%]; thickness h2SNP=1% [0–5%], h2twin=16% [5–27%]).
source: Although heritability of the global measures for each hemisphere was high (area h2SNP ~67%, h2twin ~92%; thickness h2SNP ~36%, h2twin ~81%), heritability of global asymmetry measures was substantially lower (area h2SNP=7% [95% CI=3–10%], h2twin=16% [5–27%]; thickness h2SNP=1% [0–5%], h2twin=16% [5–27%]).
evidence: This claim is supported by the heritability analysis.

claim: Four areal asymmetries showed significant twin-based heritability in HCP (leftward SMG/perisylvian and anterior insula, and rightward cingulate and STS), all of which were also significant in the SNP-based analyses (h2twin range = 19–27%; h2SNP range = 8–19%).
source: Of our robust asymmetry clusters, four areal asymmetries showed significant twin-based heritability in HCP (post-correction; leftward SMG/perisylvian and anterior insula, and rightward cingulate and STS), all of which were also significant in the SNP-based analyses (h2twin range = 19–27%; h2SNP range = 8–19%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the heritability analysis.

claim: SNP-based analyses revealed 9/14 (64%) areal asymmetry clusters exhibited significant heritability.
source: Additionally, SNP-based analyses revealed 9/14 (64%) areal asymmetry clusters exhibited significant heritability (post-correction; Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SNP-based heritability analysis.

claim: Highest SNP-based heritability was observed for leftward areal asymmetry in the anterior insula cluster (h2SNP = 18.6%, p<1.78e–15).
source: Importantly, highest SNP-based heritability was observed for leftward areal asymmetry in the anterior insula cluster (h2SNP = 18.6%, p<1.78e–15; see Supplementary file 1H), which was substantially higher than the next highest estimates in SMG/perisylvian (h2SNP = 10.7%, p=3.01e–9), retrosplenial cortex, gyrus rectus and the cingulate (all h2SNP = 8–10%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SNP-based heritability analysis.

claim: For thickness, two robust asymmetries survived correction in the twin-based analyses (rightward STS and lingual gyrus).
source: For thickness, two robust asymmetries survived correction in the twin-based analyses (rightward STS and lingual gyrus).
evidence: This claim is supported by the twin-based heritability analysis.

claim: Only 3/20 (15%) thickness asymmetries exhibited significant SNP-based heritability (h2SNP = 3–7%).
source: Moreover, only 3/20 (15%) thickness asymmetries exhibited significant SNP-based heritability (h2SNP = 3–7%; Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SNP-based heritability analysis.

claim: Cluster-wise heritability estimates were significantly lower for thickness asymmetry than for area using a SNP-based approach (β=–1.1, p=0.0008) but not a twin-based approach (β=–0.03, p=0.33).
source: Cluster-wise heritability estimates were significantly lower for thickness asymmetry than for area using a SNP-based approach (β=–1.1, p=0.0008) but not a twin-based approach (β=–0.03, p=0.33).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical comparison of heritability estimates.

claim: For areal asymmetry, 69 parcels survived FDR-correction in HCP, 84% (58) of which were also FDR-corrected significant in the SNP-based analysis.
source: For areal asymmetry, 69 parcels survived FDR-correction in HCP, 84% (58) of which were also FDR-corrected significant in the SNP-based analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cortex-wide heritability analysis.

claim: A total of 267 (53%) parcels exhibited significant FDR-corrected SNP-based heritability for areal asymmetry in UKB data.
source: Moreover, a total of 267 (53%) parcels exhibited significant FDR-corrected SNP-based heritability for areal asymmetry in UKB data (significant p[FDR]<0.05 parcels in each sample are depicted with black outlines in Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cortex-wide SNP-based heritability analysis presented in Figure 6A.

claim: A consistent heritability pattern for areal asymmetry was clearly evident using SNP- and twin-based data from independent samples, with higher heritability notably in anterior insula, SMG, Sylvian fissure, STS, calcarine sulcus, cingulate, medial and orbitofrontal cortex, and fusiform.
source: Beyond significance, a consistent heritability pattern for areal asymmetry was clearly evident using SNP- and twin-based data from independent samples, with higher heritability notably in anterior insula, SMG, Sylvian fissure, STS, calcarine sulcus, cingulate, medial and orbitofrontal cortex, and fusiform.
evidence: This claim is supported by the visual inspection of heritability maps in Figure 6A.

claim: This overlap was substantiated by a spatial correlation of r=0.46 between maps.
source: This overlap was substantiated by a spatial correlation of r=0.46 between maps; p<2.2e–16.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial correlation analysis.

claim: Maximum SNP-heritability was observed in anterior insula (parcel h2SNP = 16.4%; p<1.78e–15).
source: Moreover, maximum SNP-heritability (cyan parcel in Figure 6) was observed in anterior insula (parcel h2SNP = 16.4%; p<1.78e–15), confirming this region constitutes the most heritable cortical asymmetry in humans (and not improving on the cluster-based estimate).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cortex-wide SNP-based heritability analysis presented in Figure 6A.

claim: For thickness asymmetry, 15 parcels survived FDR-correction in the twin-based analysis, 7 of which were also post-corrected significant in the SNP-based analysis.
source: For thickness asymmetry, 15 parcels survived FDR-correction in the twin-based analysis, 7 of which were also post-corrected significant in the SNP-based analysis, and these were typically low estimates (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cortex-wide heritability analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Significant FDR-corrected SNP-heritability was observed in only 11% (57) of parcels for thickness asymmetry.
source: Moreover, significant FDR-corrected SNP-heritability was observed in only 11% (57) of parcels, including around superior temporal gyrus, planum temporale, the posterior insula/Sylvian fissure, anterior insula, and in orbitofrontal cortex (max h2SNP = 16.6%), along the cingulate and in medial visual cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cortex-wide SNP-based heritability analysis.

claim: We observed little obvious visual overlap in twin- and SNP-based heritability patterns for thickness asymmetry (spatial correlation was significant but low; r=0.24; p=0.01).
source: Beyond significance, we observed little obvious visual overlap in twin- and SNP-based heritability patterns (spatial correlation was significant but low; r=0.24; p=0.01), and higher estimates pertained to regions that were limited in extent but generally showed no clear global pattern common to both datasets, with the possible exception of calcarine, cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial correlation analysis.

claim: Cortex-wide heritability estimates were significantly lower for thickness asymmetry than for area using both a SNP-based (β=–0.71, p<2.2e–16) and twin-based approach (β=–0.33, p=1.08e–7).
source: Furthermore, cortex-wide heritability estimates were significantly lower for thickness asymmetry than for area using both a SNP-based (β=–0.71, p<2.2e–16) and twin-based approach (β=–0.33, p=1.08e–7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical comparison of cortex-wide heritability estimates.

claim: For area, SNP-based genetic correlations explained several phenotypic correlations.
source: For areal asymmetry, large SNP-based genetic correlations explained several phenotypic correlations evident in Figure 5A (Figure 6C–D; Methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic correlation analysis presented in Figure 6C.

claim: High SNP-based genetic correlations were found between leftward asymmetry in SMG/perisylvian and higher rightward asymmetry in lateral parietal cortex (LPC; rGSNP = 0.83; p[FDR]=6.58e–5).
source: For example, high SNP-based genetic correlations were found between leftward asymmetry in SMG/perisylvian and higher rightward asymmetry in lateral parietal cortex (LPC; rGSNP = 0.83; p[FDR]=6.58e–5), between leftward superior frontal cortex asymmetry and rightward asymmetry along the cingulate (rGSNP = 0.82; p[FDR]=0.01), and between leftward anterior temporal/parahippocampal asymmetry and rightward asymmetry in LPC (rGSNP = 0.68; p[FDR]=0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SNP-based genetic correlation analysis.

claim: Only one post-corrected significant SNP-based genetic correlation was found for thickness asymmetry (rGSNP = 0.68; p[FDR]=0.03).
source: In contrast, only one post-corrected significant SNP-based genetic correlation was found for thickness asymmetry (see Figure 6C; rGSNP = 0.68; p[FDR]=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SNP-based genetic correlation analysis presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Two twin-based genetic correlations survived FDR-correction, both for areal asymmetry.
source: We tested replication in the twin-based HCP sample across all cluster-pairs tested in the SNP-based analysis (Methods; note not all of these exhibited significant twin-based heritability; Supplementary file 1H-I). Two twin-based genetic correlations survived FDR-correction, both for areal asymmetry (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the twin-based genetic correlation analysis presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: One was the high genetic correlation between leftward SMG/perisylvian and rightward LPC areal asymmetry observed in the SNP-based analysis (rGtwin = 1.0 [95% CI=0.69–1.0], p[FDR] = 0.03).
source: One was the high genetic correlation between leftward SMG/perisylvian and rightward LPC areal asymmetry observed in the SNP-based analysis (rGtwin = 1.0 [95% CI=0.69–1.0], p[FDR] = 0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by the twin-based genetic correlation analysis.

claim: Higher areal asymmetry in the largest leftward cluster (SMG/perisylvian) was significantly associated with better cognition (β=0.03 [CI = 0.02 –0.04], p=7.4e–7).
source: Notably, all effect sizes were small. For general cognitive ability, we found one association, wherein higher areal asymmetry in the largest leftward cluster (SMG/perisylvian) was significantly associated with better cognition (β=0.03 [CI = 0.02 –0.04], p=7.4e–7, Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the association analysis in UK Biobank data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Reduced leftward areal asymmetry in anterior insula and thickness asymmetry along postcentral gyrus was evident in left-handers.
source: For handedness, reduced leftward areal asymmetry in anterior insula and thickness asymmetry along postcentral gyrus was evident in left-handers, in line with our recent vertex-wise mapping in UKB (Sha et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the association analysis in UK Biobank data and citation to prior work.

claim: Males typically exhibited slightly stronger areal asymmetry in large clusters (e.g. leftward SMG/perisylvian and temporal pole; rightward inferior parietal and superior frontal) but reduced leftward and rightward asymmetry in mPFC.
source: For sex effects, which were also small, males typically exhibited slightly stronger areal asymmetry in large clusters (e.g. leftward SMG/perisylvian and temporal pole; rightward inferior parietal and superior frontal) but reduced leftward and rightward asymmetry in mPFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by the association analysis in UK Biobank data.

claim: For thickness, males exhibited more rightward asymmetry in STS and posterior insula, more leftward thickness asymmetry in superior frontal cortex, but reduced rightward thickness asymmetry in entorhinal cortex and anterior insula, and reduced leftward asymmetry in caudal superior frontal cortex.
source: For thickness, males exhibited more rightward asymmetry in STS and posterior insula, more leftward thickness asymmetry in superior frontal cortex, but reduced rightward thickness asymmetry in entorhinal cortex and anterior insula, and reduced leftward asymmetry in caudal superior frontal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the association analysis in UK Biobank data.

claim: Our vertex-wise analysis of cortical asymmetries that reproduce across adult cohorts replicates and completes a recent low-resolution meta-analysis.
source: Our vertex-wise analysis of cortical asymmetries that reproduce across adult cohorts replicates and completes a recent low-resolution meta-analysis (Kong et al., 2018), and can serve as a high-fidelity phenotype for future brain asymmetry studies.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the results in relation to prior literature.

claim: The marked consistency across samples suggests consensus may now be reached regarding cortical asymmetry phenotypes in humans.
source: The marked consistency across samples suggests consensus may now be reached regarding cortical asymmetry phenotypes in humans, as our results agree with most reported results for areal asymmetry (Kong et al., 2018; Chiarello et al., 2016; Lyttelton et al., 2009; Maingault et al., 2016; Li et al., 2014), as well as several, typically more recent reports for thickness asymmetry (Kong et al., 2018; Roe et al., 2021; Li et al., 2015; Plessen et al., 2014; but see Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Limitations for an outstanding issue regarding the biological origin of thickness asymmetry).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the results in relation to prior literature.

claim: The high overlap in effects between seven datasets from four countries here suggests these results likely apply universally.
source: The high overlap in effects between seven datasets from four countries here suggests these results likely apply universally.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the replication across multiple international datasets.

claim: This evident consensus suggests genetic-developmental programs regulate mean brain lateralization with respect to both area and apparent thickness in humans.
source: This evident consensus suggests genetic-developmental programs regulate mean brain lateralization with respect to both area and apparent thickness in humans.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the consistency of asymmetry patterns across samples.

claim: The genetic findings presented herein suggest these may have reached population fixation, as heritability of even our optimally delineated asymmetry measures was generally low.
source: However, the genetic findings presented herein suggest these may have reached population fixation, as heritability of even our optimally delineated asymmetry measures was generally low.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the heritability results.

claim: This indicates either subject-specific stochastic mechanisms in early neurodevelopment or later developmental influences primarily determine cortical asymmetry.
source: This indicates either subject-specific stochastic mechanisms in early neurodevelopment or later developmental influences primarily determine cortical asymmetry.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the low heritability findings.

claim: One interpretation of lifespan stability combined with low heritability may be stochastic early-life developmental influences determine individual differences in areal asymmetry more than later developmental change.
source: One interpretation of lifespan stability combined with low heritability may be stochastic early-life developmental influences determine individual differences in areal asymmetry more than later developmental change, but work linking prenatal and childhood trajectories is needed to affirm this.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: Childhood development of thickness asymmetry until a peak around age ~24, higher directional variability in adult samples, and lower heritability all converge to suggest thickness asymmetry may be more shaped through subject-specific effects in later childhood, possibly through interaction with the environment.
source: In contrast, childhood development of thickness asymmetry until a peak around age ~24 (Roe et al., 2021), higher directional variability in adult samples, and lower heritability all converge to suggest thickness asymmetry may be more shaped through subject-specific effects in later childhood, possibly through interaction with the environment.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined findings for thickness asymmetry.

claim: This interpretation applied to asymmetry also agrees with work suggesting cortical area in general may trace more to early-life factors whereas thickness may be more impacted by lifespan influences.
source: This interpretation applied to asymmetry also agrees with work suggesting cortical area in general may trace more to early-life factors (Walhovd et al., 2016; Grasby et al., 2020; Rakic, 1995) whereas thickness may be more impacted by lifespan influences (Grasby et al., 2020; Fjell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: For areal asymmetry, adult-like patterns of lateralization were strongly established before age ~4, indicating areal asymmetry traces back further and does not primarily emerge through later cortical expansion.
source: For areal asymmetry, adult-like patterns of lateralization were strongly established before age ~4, indicating areal asymmetry traces back further and does not primarily emerge through later cortical expansion (Wierenga et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the lifespan trajectory findings.

claim: This may align with evidence indicating areal asymmetry may be primarily determined in utero.
source: This may align with evidence indicating areal asymmetry may be primarily determined in utero (Li et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2023), including evidence suggesting little change in areal asymmetry from birth to 2 years (Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Wierenga et al., 2014), and little difference between maps derived from neonates and adults (Li et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It may also fit with the principle that the primary microstructural basis of cortical area – the number of and spacing between cortical minicolumns – is determined in prenatal life.
source: It may also fit with the principle that the primary microstructural basis of cortical area (Rakic, 1995) – the number of and spacing between cortical minicolumns – is determined in prenatal life (Rakic, 1995; Fjell et al., 2019), and agree with work suggesting asymmetry at this microstructural level may underly hemispheric differences in surface area (Chance et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Our results may therefore constrain the extent to which areal asymmetry can be viewed as a plastic feature of brain organization.
source: Our results may therefore constrain the extent to which areal asymmetry can be viewed as a plastic feature of brain organization, and may even suggest areal asymmetry may sometimes be a marker for innate hemispheric specializations shared by most humans.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The degree of precision with which leftward areal asymmetry follows the contours of auditory regions in the Sylvian fissure that show left functional lateralization may be one example.
source: Although future research is needed to assess structure-function relationships, the degree of precision with which leftward areal asymmetry follows the contours of auditory regions in the Sylvian fissure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) that show left functional lateralization may be one example (Chance et al., 2006; Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2018; Ocklenburg et al., 2018); we found ~94% of individuals exhibited leftward areal asymmetry here – the most consistently lateralized cortical region in humans (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior literature and data from Figure 1.

claim: Developmental trajectories showed non-linear asymmetry growth by virtue of accelerated thinning of the non-dominant hemisphere.
source: Developmental trajectories showed non-linear asymmetry growth by virtue of accelerated thinning of the non-dominant hemisphere (10/20 clusters showed this relative hemispheric difference in the rate of developmental thinning; Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the developmental trajectory analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: These trajectories clearly suggest differentiation of the cortex occurs with respect to thickness asymmetry in development, possibly (though not necessarily) suggesting it may be more amenable to experience-dependent change.
source: These trajectories clearly suggest differentiation of the cortex occurs with respect to thickness asymmetry in development, possibly (though not necessarily) suggesting it may be more amenable to experience-dependent change.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the developmental trajectory findings.

claim: As cortical thinning in childhood is thought to partly reflect learning-dependent processes such as intracortical myelination, pruning of initially overproduced synapses and neuropil reduction, thickness asymmetry growth may suggest hemispheric differences in the developmental optimization of cortical networks at least partly shaped by childhood experience.
source: Indeed, as cortical thinning in childhood is thought to partly reflect learning-dependent processes such as intracortical myelination (Natu et al., 2019), pruning of initially overproduced synapses (Petanjek et al., 2011; Faust et al., 2021) and neuropil reduction, thickness asymmetry growth may suggest hemispheric differences in the developmental optimization of cortical networks at least partly shaped by childhood experience.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: This raises the possibility thickness asymmetry may be a marker of ontogenetic hemispheric specialization within neurocognitive networks, possibly in line with animal models suggesting lateralized training can alter the balance in homotopic thickness.
source: This raises the possibility thickness asymmetry may be a marker of ontogenetic hemispheric specialization within neurocognitive networks, possibly in line with animal models suggesting lateralized training can alter the balance in homotopic thickness (Díaz et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: However, this is speculative, and intervention approaches are needed to experimentally test plasticity of thickness asymmetry in humans.
source: However, this is speculative, and intervention approaches are needed to experimentally test plasticity of thickness asymmetry in humans.
evidence: This claim acknowledges the speculative nature of the interpretation and calls for future research.

claim: Our findings agree with work finding a similar left-right thickness asymmetry pattern shows rapid longitudinal increase in the first years of life, particularly in mPFC.
source: However, our findings agree with work finding a similar left-right thickness asymmetry pattern shows rapid longitudinal increase in the first years of life (Li et al., 2015), particularly in mPFC (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: As we observed rapid asymmetry differentiation spanning childhood and adolescence in most prefrontal regions and others, we extend these earlier findings in neonates.
source: As we observed rapid asymmetry differentiation spanninng childhood and adolescence in most prefrontal regions and others (Figure 3; Figure 4; Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4), we extend these earlier findings in neonates (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the findings in relation to prior literature.

claim: Likely, longitudinal data and nonlinear modelling was critical to capture early developmental growth in thickness asymmetry within a lifespan perspective.
source: Likely, longitudinal data and nonlinear modelling was critical to capture early developmental growth in thickness asymmetry within a lifespan perspective, because large variation in hemispheric thickness estimates at any age may hinder detection of subtle change effects even in large cross-sectional samples (Fjell et al., 2020), rendering follow-up data likely critical in the context of cortical asymmetry change.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the methodological requirements for detecting the observed effects.

claim: As prefrontal thickness asymmetry seems particularly vulnerable in some neurodevelopmental disorders, aging, and Alzheimer's disease, these trajectories provide a useful normative reference regarding the timing of expected brain change in development.
source: As prefrontal thickness asymmetry seems particularly vulnerable in some neurodevelopmental disorders (Postema et al., 2019), aging, and Alzheimer's disease (Roe et al., 2021), these trajectories provide a useful normative reference regarding the timing of expected brain change in development.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the implications of the findings, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most clusters delineated here did not exhibit the relative hemispheric difference in rates of cortical thinning we have previously shown is a feature of aging in heteromodal cortex, except in clusters overlapping with our previous analysis.
source: With regards to aging, most clusters delineated here did not exhibit the relative hemispheric difference in rates of cortical thinning we have previously shown is a feature of aging in heteromodal cortex (Roe et al., 2021), except in clusters overlapping with our previous analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the aging trajectory analysis and citation to prior work.

claim: This fits with our previous work showing aging-related loss in thickness asymmetry is specific to heteromodal regions vulnerable in aging.
source: This fits with our previous work showing aging-related loss in thickness asymmetry is specific to heteromodal regions vulnerable in aging.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Developmental differentiation and aging-related dedifferentiation of thickness asymmetry underscores its proposed role in supporting optimal brain organization and function.
source: Developmental differentiation and aging-related dedifferentiation of thickness asymmetry underscores its proposed role in supporting optimal brain organization and function, though it seems not all thickness asymmetries that grow in childhood development decline in aging.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined developmental and aging findings.

claim: In general, this fit with a multifaceted view, in which most asymmetries were either not or only weakly correlated – but reliably so – contrasting views emphasizing a single biological or overall anatomical factor controlling cerebral lateralization.
source: In general, this fit with a multifaceted view (Bain et al., 2019; Rentería, 2012; Francks, 2015), in which most asymmetries were either not or only weakly correlated – but reliably so – contrasting views emphasizing a single biological (Annett, 1998; Annett, 1964) or overall anatomical factor (Crow, 2010) controlling cerebral lateralization.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the interregional correlation findings in relation to prior theories.

claim: However, we also identified several regions wherein areal asymmetry reliably correlated within individuals, showing the variance in cortical asymmetries is not always dissociable, as often thought.
source: However, we also identified several regions wherein areal asymmetry reliably correlated within individuals, showing the variance in cortical asymmetries is not always dissociable, as often thought (Bain et al., 2019; Rentería, 2012; Francks, 2015).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the interregional correlation findings.

claim: Several of these were underpinned by high asymmetry-asymmetry SNP-based genetic correlations, illustrating some lateralizations in surface area exhibit coordinated genetic development.
source: Several of these were underpinned by high asymmetry-asymmetry SNP-based genetic correlations, illustrating some lateralizations in surface area exhibit coordinated genetic development.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the genetic correlation findings.

claim: These data for thickness indicate individuals may tend towards either leftward asymmetry, rightward asymmetry, or symmetry, both globally across the cortex and irrespective of the region-specific average direction of asymmetry.
source: These data for thickness indicate individuals may tend towards either leftward asymmetry, rightward asymmetry, or symmetry, both globally across the cortex and irrespective of the region-specific average direction of asymmetry (Figure 5—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the thickness asymmetry correlation findings.

claim: This result may be in broad agreement with the notion that some lateralized genetic-developmental programs may trigger lateralization in either direction or lose their directional bias through environmental interaction.
source: This result may be in broad agreement with the notion that some lateralized genetic-developmental programs may trigger lateralization in either direction or lose their directional bias through environmental interaction (Francks, 2015).
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: As thickness asymmetry seems established at but minimal from birth, genetic effects may determine the average region-specific hemispheric bias in the population, but later developmental change may subsequently confer major increases upon its directional variance.
source: As thickness asymmetry seems established at but minimal from birth (Li et al., 2015), genetic effects may determine the average region-specific hemispheric bias in the population, but later developmental change may subsequently confer major increases upon its directional variance (Francks, 2015).
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Overall, our data suggests developmental change in thickness asymmetry may lead to directional variability of its lateralization across individuals.
source: Overall, our data suggests developmental change in thickness asymmetry may lead to directional variability of its lateralization across individuals.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: Thus, far from being independent phenotypes, thickness asymmetries may be globally interrelated across cortex and their direction coordinated through childhood.
source: Thus, far from being independent phenotypes (Bain et al., 2019; Rentería, 2012), thickness asymmetries may be globally interrelated across cortex and their direction coordinated through childhood.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the findings in relation to prior views.

claim: We also found areal asymmetry in anterior insula is, to our knowledge, the most heritable asymmetry yet reported with genomic methods.
source: We also found areal asymmetry in anterior insula is, to our knowledge, the most heritable asymmetry yet reported with genomic methods (Sha et al., 2021a; Sha et al., 2021b; Carrion-Castillo et al., 2020; Cuellar-Partida et al., 2021; Elliott et al., 2018), with common SNPs explaining ~19% variance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the heritability analysis and citations to prior literature.

claim: This is notably higher than in our recent report (<5%).
source: This is notably higher than in our recent report (<5%) (Sha et al., 2021a), illustrating a benefit of our approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior work.

claim: Highest SNP and twin-based heritability for areal asymmetry was found in regions constituting the earliest emerging cortical asymmetries in utero.
source: Furthermore, highest SNP and twin-based heritability for areal asymmetry was found in regions constituting the earliest emerging cortical asymmetries in utero (Dubois et al., 2010; Habas et al., 2012; Kasprian et al., 2011; Hill et al., 2010): anterior insula, STS, PT, medial occipital cortex, and parahippocampal gyrus (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the heritability findings in relation to prior literature on prenatal development.

claim: The effects agree with and elaborate on two previous genetic explorations and reports of heritable areal asymmetry in handedness-associated clusters.
source: The effects agree with and elaborate on two previous genetic explorations (Kong et al., 2018; Sha et al., 2021b) and reports of heritable areal asymmetry in handedness-associated clusters (Sha et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the findings in relation to prior literature.

claim: However, while heritability of either hemisphere was high, areal asymmetry heritability was still only moderate at best, suggesting genetic but primarily subject-specific stochastic effects underly its formation.
source: However, while heritability of either hemisphere was high, areal asymmetry heritability was still only moderate at best, suggesting genetic but primarily subject-specific stochastic effects underly its formation.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the heritability findings.

claim: By contrast, thickness asymmetry was generally not heritable, or showed low and localized heritability effects with no clear global pattern, as well as more divergent results using twin and genomic methods, possibly due to low-power for twin-models.
source: By contrast, thickness asymmetry was generally not heritable, or showed low and localized heritability effects with no clear global pattern, as well as more divergent results using twin and genomic methods, possibly due to low-power for twin-models.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the heritability findings.

claim: Together, lifespan stability, higher heritability, and phenotypic and genetic correlations suggest higher genetic influence upon individual differences in areal asymmetry.
source: Together, lifespan stability (Li et al., 2014), higher heritability, and phenotypic and genetic correlations suggest higher genetic influence upon individual differences in areal asymmetry.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: By contrast, childhood developmental growth, directional variability and low heritability suggest thickness asymmetry may be more shaped through individual lifespan exposures.
source: By contrast, childhood developmental growth, directional variability and low heritability suggest thickness asymmetry may be more shaped through individual lifespan exposures (Fjell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: Whether region-specific thickness asymmetry change relates to the maturation of lateralized brain functions is thus an interesting question for future research.
source: Whether region-specific thickness asymmetry change relates to the maturation of lateralized brain functions is thus an interesting question for future research (Bishop and Bates, 2019; Somers et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is a suggestion for future research supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: These results support a differentiation between early-life (i.e. before age ~4) and later developmental factors in shaping areal and thickness asymmetry, respectively.
source: Regardless, these results support a differentiation between early-life (i.e. before age ~4) and later developmental factors in shaping areal and thickness asymmetry, respectively.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: Since interhemispheric anatomy here is likely related to brain torque, this may agree with work suggesting torque relates to cognitive outcomes.
source: Since interhemispheric anatomy here is likely related to brain torque (Toga and Thompson, 2003; LeMay, 1976), this may agree with work suggesting torque relates to cognitive outcomes (Kong, 2019; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Interestingly, that ~94% of humans exhibit leftward asymmetry in this region suggests tightly regulated genetic-developmental programs control its lateralized direction in humans.
source: Interestingly, that ~94% of humans exhibit leftward asymmetry in this region (Figure 1G) suggests tightly regulated genetic-developmental programs control its lateralized direction in humans (see Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the high proportion of individuals showing the same direction of asymmetry.

claim: This result may therefore suggest disruptions in areal lateralization early in life are associated with cognitive deficits detectable in later life as small effects in big data.
source: This result may therefore suggest disruptions in areal lateralization early in life are associated with cognitive deficits detectable in later life as small effects in big data (Deary et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: While speculative, this may also agree with evidence that differences in general cognitive ability that show high lifespan stability relate primarily to areal phenotypes formed early in life.
source: While speculative, this may also agree with evidence that differences in general cognitive ability that show high lifespan stability (Deary et al., 2004) relate primarily to areal phenotypes formed early in life (Walhovd et al., 2016; Rakic, 1995; Fjell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Anterior insula lies within a left-lateralized functional language network, and its structural asymmetry may relate to language lateralization in which left-handers show increased atypicality.
source: Anterior insula lies within a left-lateralized functional language network (Labache et al., 2019), and its structural asymmetry may relate to language lateralization (Chiarello et al., 2013; Biduła and Króliczak, 2015; Keller et al., 2011) in which left-handers show increased atypicality (Wiberg et al., 2019; Mazoyer et al., 2014; Westerhausen et al., 2006; Carey and Johnstone, 2014).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Since asymmetry here emerges early in utero and is by far the most heritable, we agree with others that this ontogenetically foundational region of cortex may be fruitful for understanding genetic-developmental mechanisms influencing laterality.
source: Since asymmetry here emerges early in utero (Dubois et al., 2010) and is by far the most heritable (Figure 6), we agree with others (Chiarello et al., 2013) that this ontogenetically foundational region of cortex may be fruitful for understanding genetic-developmental mechanisms influencing laterality (Afif et al., 2007; Kalani et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Less leftward somatosensory thickness asymmetry in left-handers also echoes our recent report and fits a scenario whereby thickness asymmetries may be partly shaped through use-dependent plasticity and detectable through group-level hemispheric specializations of function.
source: Less leftward somatosensory thickness asymmetry in left-handers also echoes our recent report (Sha et al., 2021a) and fits a scenario whereby thickness asymmetries may be partly shaped through use-dependent plasticity and detectable through group-level hemispheric specializations of function.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Still, the small effects show cortical asymmetry cannot predict individual handedness.
source: Still, the small effects show cortical asymmetry cannot predict individual handedness.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the small effect sizes found.

claim: Associations with other factors typically assumed important were similarly small, and mostly compatible with the ENIGMA report and elsewhere.
source: Associations with other factors typically assumed important were similarly small, and mostly compatible with the ENIGMA report (Kong et al., 2018) and elsewhere (Williams et al., 2022; Guadalupe et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the findings in relation to prior literature.

claim: Possibly, differences in sample median age (UKB = ~64; Kong et al., 2018 = 26) and potential sex-differences in brain decline may underlie some inconsistencies.
source: Possibly, differences in sample median age (UKB = ~64; Kong et al., 2018 = 26) and potential sex-differences in brain decline (McCarrey et al., 2016) may underlie some inconsistencies.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of inconsistencies with prior literature.
